column6: David answers Goliath that he comes in the name of YHWH before acting in battle. It is a direct Hebrew Bible instance of a concrete, otherwise ordinary act explicitly placed under the divine name.
Peter commands the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ. This supplies a New Testament instance of the commentary's bi-ism relation functioning as the means or accompaniment of an act.
The name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are protected. It closely joins the commentary's divine name, Noah's protective enclosure, and mercy as a place of refuge.

column5: putting the name upon a people
column6: The priests put YHWH's name upon Israel and God blesses them. This makes the name an identifying, protective inscription on a community, extending the commentary's owner-mark image.
The command not to profane YHWH's holy name but to sanctify it among Israel gives a Torah counterpart to the commentary's raised name and to prayer's opening hallowing of God.

column5: name dwelling where offerings are brought
column6: The sanctuary is the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, and Israel brings its offerings there. This directly joins named divine presence, a house, and the sacrificial animals discussed in the commentary.

The text directs Israel's slaughtered animals to be brought to YHWH as sacrifices rather than left in the open field. It is a concrete Torah companion to the commentary's meat whose ritual character depends on the one named over it.

Food is said to be sanctified through God's word and prayer. This offers a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that the divine reference over food changes its status without changing its substance.

column5: food entering a person and defilement
column6: Jesus says that what enters from outside cannot defile a person. Read beside the commentary's named-slaughter material, it supplies a focused alternative account of how food is or is not religiously altered.

YHWH desires steadfast love and knowledge of God rather than sacrifice. Its contrast closely supports the commentary's claim that moral God-consciousness, not animal material, is what matters in offering.

The makers of the calf name it as the god or gods who brought Israel from Egypt. This is the core Biblical scene behind the commentary's calf episode, where a manufactured object displaces the merciful Lord.

column5: who belongs to YHWH after the calf
column6: Moses' call, "Who is for YHWH?", turns the calf crisis into a test of exclusive allegiance. It sharpens the commentary's link between the divine name, worship, and refusal of rival names.

Job describes the heart being enticed by the shining sun or splendid moon and the hand sent a kiss. It gives a vivid Hebrew Bible parallel to the commentary's celestial images and its warning against treating them as gods.
God places the lights in the sky for signs, appointed times, days, and years. This is a creation account counterpart to the commentary's visible crescent as a calendrical sign.

column5: pain in carrying and giving birth
column6: The woman's pain in childbearing gives a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the womb that bears and nourishes also bears the cost of birth.
A nearest relative is charged to redeem a brother's land when he becomes poor. This gives legal concreteness to the commentary's move from common womb to obligations of kinship.

God's compassion is stirred while anger against Ephraim is held back. It closely accompanies the commentary's Rahman/Rahim and wrath tension, especially its calf scene in which anger turns toward mercy.
Paul says that all have been enclosed in disobedience so that God may have mercy on all. This gives a Christian formulation of mercy's widest scope while retaining an account of disobedience.

column5: Son sent and born of a woman
column6: Paul says God sent his Son, born of a woman. The verse pairs divine sonship with human birth and therefore stands directly beside the commentary's womb-rooted mercy and rejection of divine child-taking.
The name of the God of Jacob protects the petitioner in a day of trouble. This is a separate Biblical instance of the commentary's name as a refuge rather than only an address or oath.
Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name. It gives a specifically Christian development of the commentary's idea that entry under the divine name is a sphere of preservation.

column5: teaching as rain that makes growth
column6: Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on grass and vegetation. It meets the commentary's secondary cloud-water-growth image and its association of divine instruction with life-giving nurture.

column5: voyage brought to a desired haven
column6: After the storm is quieted, God brings sailors to their desired haven. This is a concrete Biblical meeting with the commentary's concern for a ship's movement and its safe coming to rest.

column5: sign on hand, memorial, and speech
column6: The exodus observance is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction is in the mouth. It brings together visible mark, remembrance, and spoken devotion in a way that complements the commentary's name-as-sign.

column5: mercy attributes recited as a prayer order
column6: The Talmud portrays God showing Moses the order for invoking the mercy attributes when Israel sins. This makes the Exodus mercy-name formula a repeated liturgical opening, a close Jewish interpretive companion to the recited Fatiha.

column5: mercy toward creatures and mercy from heaven
column6: The maxim that one who has mercy on creatures receives mercy from Heaven turns divine compassion into a directed human ethic, parallel to the commentary's Rahim as mercy reaching particular vulnerable beings.

column5: witnessed appearance of the new moon
column6: The mishnah's procedure for father-and-son witnesses who saw the new moon makes communal testimony depend on the newly visible lunar form. It is a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's rising crescent becoming a recognized sign.
